slides.sub: Benjamin West, The Death of General Wolfe, 1770

slides.headline: Quebec, 1759
slides.text: 13 September 1759, outside Quebec. Britain and France are fighting for North America. The British general, James Wolfe, has just been shot.

slides.headline: The dying general
slides.text: Wolfe lies in the arms of his officers, pale, eyes turned to heaven, posed almost like Christ taken down from the cross.

slides.headline: The news
slides.text: On the left, a ranger points to the distant battle. News is coming: the French are retreating. Legend says Wolfe heard it before dying.

slides.headline: The warrior
slides.text: In front, a Native warrior kneels, chin on his fist, watching Wolfe in silence, the calmest witness in the scene.

slides.headline: The witnesses
slides.text: All around, officers grieve, each face a real portrait. But here is the twist: of these fourteen men, only four were actually there.

slides.headline: Modern clothes
slides.text: Even more shocking then: real modern uniforms. Joshua Reynolds urged West to dress them like ancient heroes. West refused.

slides.headline: The king says no
slides.text: King George III would not buy it: modern uniforms seemed undignified for a hero. Yet a year later, he ordered his own copy.

slides.headline: Truth or legend?
slides.text: West invented witnesses to build a perfect hero, and it worked: this is how the world remembers Wolfe. Can a painting lie?
